FROM actor a
         JOIN film_actor fa ON fa.actor_id = a.actor_id

changes.title: how many films are short, medium, long, or of unknown length
request: Put each film in one of four groups by its `length`: `short` under 60 minutes, `medium` from 60 to 120 minutes, `long` over 120 minutes, and `unknown` where `length` is NULL.
Show each group with its number of films, from the shortest group to the longest, `unknown` last.
A `CASE` expression makes the group, and the query groups by it; a NULL length passes no comparison, so it needs a test of its own.
changes.sql:
SELECT CASE
           WHEN length IS NULL THEN 'unknown'
           WHEN length < 60 THEN 'short'
           WHEN length <= 120 THEN 'medium'
           ELSE 'long'
           END  AS size,
       COUNT(*) AS films
FROM film
GROUP BY size
ORDER BY CASE size WHEN 'short' THEN 1 WHEN 'medium' THEN 2 WHEN 'long' THEN 3 ELSE 4 END

       (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM film)      AS film,

        FROM film f
        WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM film_text ft WHERE ft.film_id = f.film_id)) AS without_text,

        FROM film_text ft

       COUNT(i.inventory_id) AS copies,
       COUNT(CASE
                 WHEN i.inventory_id IS NOT NULL
                     AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1
                                     FROM rental r

FROM (SELECT 'Trailers' AS feature
      UNION ALL
      SELECT 'Commentaries'
      UNION ALL
      SELECT 'Deleted Scenes'
      UNION ALL

         LEFT JOIN film f ON FIND_IN_SET(sf.feature, f.special_features) > 0

ORDER BY films DESC, sf.feature

changes.title: how many films use each language, as language and as original language
changes.file_header: Exercises at the advanced level on language: references turned into rows with UNION ALL, and counted under conditions. Each poses a question, answers it, and shows what the installed data gives back.
request: For every language, even one no film uses, count the films that use it as their `language_id` and the films that use it as their `original_language_id`, both in one row, ordered by `language_id`.
A `UNION ALL` turns the two references into rows, each tagged with its role, and a `COUNT` of a `CASE` counts each role.

SELECT l.*,
       COUNT(CASE WHEN u.role = 'language' THEN 1 END) AS as_language,
       COUNT(CASE WHEN u.role = 'original' THEN 1 END) AS as_original_language
FROM language l
         LEFT JOIN (SELECT language_id, 'language' AS role
                    FROM film
                    UNION ALL
                    SELECT original_language_id, 'original'
                    FROM film
                    WHERE original_language_id IS NOT NULL) u ON u.language_id = l.language_id
GROUP BY l.language_id
ORDER BY l.language_id

changes.title: the films with the most actors in each category
changes.file_header: Exercises at the advanced level on film_list: a window function over the view's rows. Each poses a question, answers it, and shows what the installed data gives back.
request: Count each film's actors from the view's `actors` string, one more than its commas, or `0` when it is `NULL`.
In each category, find the films with the most actors, all of them when several tie.
Show the `category`, `FID`, `title` and the number of actors, ordered by `category` and then by `FID`.
`RANK()` over each category keeps the ties.
changes.sql:
WITH counted AS (SELECT category,
                        FID,
                        title,
                        CASE WHEN actors IS NULL THEN 0
                             ELSE LENGTH(actors) - LENGTH(REPLACE(actors, ',', '')) + 1 END AS actor_count
                 FROM film_list)
SELECT category, FID, title, actor_count
FROM (SELECT counted.*, RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY category ORDER BY actor_count DESC) AS actor_rank
      FROM counted) ranked
WHERE actor_rank = 1
ORDER BY category, FID

changes.title: the ten copies most overdue, as of the last rental
request: Take the date of the last rental in the data as now.
A copy is overdue when its open rental, with no `return_date`, is older than its film's `rental_duration` in days.
Show the ten most overdue: the `rental_id`, the `inventory_id`, the film's `title`, the `rental_date` and the days overdue, the most first; ties are ordered by `rental_id`.
changes.sql:
SELECT r.rental_id,
       i.inventory_id,
       f.title,
       r.rental_date,
       DATEDIFF(m.last_rental, r.rental_date) - f.rental_duration AS days_overdue
FROM rental r
         JOIN inventory i ON i.inventory_id = r.inventory_id
         JOIN film f ON f.film_id = i.film_id
         CROSS JOIN (SELECT MAX(rental_date) AS last_rental FROM rental) m
WHERE r.return_date IS NULL
  AND r.rental_date + INTERVAL f.rental_duration DAY < m.last_rental
ORDER BY days_overdue DESC, r.rental_id
LIMIT 10

changes._why: the view hides the store; subtotals with WITH ROLLUP and GROUPING() check its totals against the tables
changes.title: each category's sales at each store, with the view's total beside them
request: Sum the payments of each category at each store, through rental, copy and `film_category`, with a subtotal for each category and a grand total.
Show the `category`, the `store_id`, the sales and, on each category's subtotal row, the view's `total_sales`, which should be equal.
Order by the category, then by the store, with the subtotal after its stores and the grand total last.
`WITH ROLLUP` adds the subtotal rows, and `GROUPING()` tells them from the others.
changes.sql:
SELECT g.category, g.store_id, g.sales, s.total_sales
FROM (SELECT c.name                AS category,
             i.store_id,
             SUM(p.amount)         AS sales,
             GROUPING(c.name)      AS g_category,
             GROUPING(i.store_id)  AS g_store
      FROM payment p
               JOIN rental r ON r.rental_id = p.rental_id
               JOIN inventory i ON i.inventory_id = r.inventory_id
               JOIN film_category fc ON fc.film_id = i.film_id
               JOIN category c ON c.category_id = fc.category_id
      GROUP BY c.name, i.store_id
      WITH ROLLUP) g
         LEFT JOIN sales_by_film_category s ON s.category = g.category AND g.g_store = 1
ORDER BY g.g_category, g.category, g.g_store, g.store_id

Join each row to its store, the store's address, city and country, and show the `ID`, `name`, where they live, where they work, and whether the two are the same city of the same country, ordered by `ID`.
City names repeat across countries, so the comparison takes the country too.

SELECT l.*,
       ci.city                                        AS store_city,
       co.country                                     AS store_country,
       (l.city = ci.city AND l.country = co.country) AS lives_in_store_city
FROM staff_list l
         JOIN store st ON st.store_id = l.SID
         JOIN address a ON a.address_id = st.address_id
         JOIN city ci ON ci.city_id = a.city_id
         JOIN country co ON co.country_id = ci.country_id

changes.sql:
SELECT st.*,
       COUNT(DISTINCT i.film_id)                  AS films,
       COUNT(DISTINCT CASE
                          WHEN NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1
                                           FROM inventory o
                                           WHERE o.film_id = i.film_id
                                             AND o.store_id <> st.store_id)
                              THEN i.film_id END) AS films_only_here
FROM store st
         LEFT JOIN inventory i ON i.store_id = st.store_id
GROUP BY st.store_id
ORDER BY st.store_id

FROM staff_list l
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1
              FROM rental r
                       JOIN customer cu ON cu.customer_id = r.customer_id

changes._why: film.rental_duration against the rental dates is the schema's own notion of lateness (get_customer_balance), and no exercise uses it per customer
changes.title: the five customers who returned late most often
request: A rental is late when it was returned more days after it was rented than its film's `rental_duration`, as `get_customer_balance` counts it.
Show the five customers with the most late returns, with their counts, the most first; ties are ordered by `customer_id`.
A rental not yet returned has no `return_date`, so it drops out of the comparison.
changes.sql:
SELECT c.*, COUNT(*) AS late_returns
FROM customer c
         JOIN rental r ON r.customer_id = c.customer_id
         JOIN inventory i ON i.inventory_id = r.inventory_id
         JOIN film f ON f.film_id = i.film_id
WHERE DATEDIFF(r.return_date, r.rental_date) > f.rental_duration
GROUP BY c.customer_id
ORDER BY late_returns DESC, c.customer_id
LIMIT 5

changes._why: no exercise uses LAG over dates, which rental_date makes natural
changes.title: the five customers with the longest gap between two rentals
request: For each customer, take the days between each rental and the customer's previous one, and keep the longest.
Show the five customers with the longest gap, with the gap in days, the longest first; ties are ordered by `customer_id`.
`LAG` gives each rental the one before it; `rental_id` breaks a tie of `rental_date`, which is not unique per customer.
changes.sql:
WITH gaps AS (SELECT r.customer_id,
                     DATEDIFF(r.rental_date,
                              LAG(r.rental_date) OVER (PARTITION BY r.customer_id ORDER BY r.rental_date, r.rental_id)) AS gap_days
              FROM rental r)
SELECT c.*, MAX(g.gap_days) AS longest_gap
FROM customer c
         JOIN gaps g ON g.customer_id = c.customer_id
GROUP BY c.customer_id
ORDER BY longest_gap DESC, c.customer_id
LIMIT 5

changes._why: the view defines name as exactly that CONCAT, so the query can never return a row
SAKILA_ADDRESS_I_03's 'none' class counts exactly these addresses; three NOT EXISTS is not Advanced either
RANK() gave a country with a tie two rows, so LIMIT 5 cut rows, not countries; the country was grouped by its name, which is not unique; no tie-break on the country's total
request: Sum each customer's payments, and their country's.

For each country, find the customer who paid the most, numbering the customers within the country with a window function (`ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY ...)`), the largest total first and ties by `customer_id`, and take the country's total with another (`SUM() OVER (PARTITION BY ...)`).

Show, for the five countries which paid the most, the country, its top customer's `customer_id`, `first_name`, `last_name` and total, and the country's total, the largest country first; ties by `country_id`.
`ROW_NUMBER` gives each country one first row, so `LIMIT 5` keeps five countries; `RANK` would give a tie two.
changes.sql:
WITH paid AS (SELECT co.country_id, co.country, cu.customer_id, cu.first_name, cu.last_name, SUM(p.amount) AS total
              FROM payment p
                       JOIN customer cu ON cu.customer_id = p.customer_id
                       JOIN address a ON a.address_id = cu.address_id
                       JOIN city ci ON ci.city_id = a.city_id
                       JOIN country co ON co.country_id = ci.country_id
              GROUP BY co.country_id, co.country, cu.customer_id, cu.first_name, cu.last_name),
     ranked AS (SELECT paid.*,
                       ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY country_id ORDER BY total DESC, customer_id) AS rank_in_country,
                       SUM(total) OVER (PARTITION BY country_id)                                   AS country_total
                FROM paid)
SELECT country, customer_id, first_name, last_name, total, country_total
FROM ranked
WHERE rank_in_country = 1
ORDER BY country_total DESC, country_id
LIMIT 5

changes._why: the payments skip months (2005-09 to 2006-01), so LAG compared February 2006 with August 2005; a calendar of months fills the gap with 0
request: Sum the payments of each month, written as `YYYY-MM`, from the first month with a payment to the last, a month without any included with `0`, and, for each month, the difference from the month before it, taken with `LAG`.
The payments skip months, so a recursive `WITH` lists every month of the span first; `LAG` over the payment months alone would compare a month with an older one.
The first month has none, so its difference is `NULL`.
Show each month with its total and the difference.
changes.sql:
WITH RECURSIVE monthly AS (SELECT CAST(DATE_FORMAT(payment_date, '%Y-%m-01') AS DATE) AS month, SUM(amount) AS total
                           FROM payment
                           GROUP BY month),
               months AS (SELECT MIN(month) AS month
                          FROM monthly
                          UNION ALL
                          SELECT month + INTERVAL 1 MONTH
                          FROM months
                          WHERE month < (SELECT MAX(month) FROM monthly))
SELECT DATE_FORMAT(m.month, '%Y-%m')                                           AS month,
       COALESCE(p.total, 0)                                                    AS total,
       COALESCE(p.total, 0) - LAG(COALESCE(p.total, 0)) OVER (ORDER BY m.month) AS change_from_previous
FROM months m
         LEFT JOIN monthly p ON p.month = m.month
ORDER BY m.month

changes._why: a NULL length fell into ELSE 'long', as in SAKILA_FILM_I_03; the same 'unknown' group
request: Sort the films into four groups by `length`: `short` under 60 minutes, `medium` from 60 to 120, `long` over 120, and `unknown` where `length` is NULL.
Count the rentals of each group's films, through the copy, and sum their payments; a rental may have no payment, so the payments are joined with an outer join.
Show each group with its count and sum, from the group of the shortest films to the group of the longest, `unknown` last.
The group is a `CASE` expression, and the statement groups by it; a rental has one payment at most, which SAKILA_PAYMENT_B_06 checks, so `COUNT(*)` counts the rentals.
changes.sql:
SELECT CASE
           WHEN f.length IS NULL THEN 'unknown'
           WHEN f.length < 60 THEN 'short'
           WHEN f.length <= 120 THEN 'medium'
           ELSE 'long'
           END       AS length_group,
       COUNT(*)      AS rentals,
       SUM(p.amount) AS total
FROM rental r
         JOIN inventory i ON i.inventory_id = r.inventory_id
         JOIN film f ON f.film_id = i.film_id
         LEFT JOIN payment p ON p.rental_id = r.rental_id
GROUP BY length_group
ORDER BY CASE length_group WHEN 'short' THEN 1 WHEN 'medium' THEN 2 WHEN 'long' THEN 3 ELSE 4 END

changes._why: 'in 2005' had no lower bound; rental_id joins the final tie-break
request: For each rental made in 2005, find the same customer's rental just before it in 2005, and the number of days between the two.

Show the five longest waits: the `customer_id`, the earlier and the later `rental_date`, and the days, the longest first; on a tie, by `customer_id`, then by the later `rental_date`, then by `rental_id`.
The rental just before is `LAG(...) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY rental_date, rental_id)`, over the rentals from January 1, 2005 up to January 1, 2006.
changes.sql:
SELECT customer_id, previous_rental, rental_date, DATEDIFF(rental_date, previous_rental) AS days
FROM (SELECT rental_id,
             customer_id,
             rental_date,
             LAG(rental_date) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY rental_date, rental_id) AS previous_rental
      FROM rental
      WHERE rental_date >= '2005-01-01'
        AND rental_date < '2006-01-01') g
WHERE previous_rental IS NOT NULL
ORDER BY days DESC, customer_id, rental_date, rental_id
LIMIT 5

FROM sales_by_store v
ORDER BY v.total_sales DESC, v.store
